name: Vwanji
confidence_why: one confirmed first-hand source; 5 other works read were silent

catalog_locator: Eaton 2018: Section 3 'Stress', p. 12 (PDF p. 12); vowel length p. 5, sec. 2.2; phonological-word diagnostics pp. 23-24. Eaton 2020: p. 66 (lines 67-69) and fn. 5 p. 67; stress-marked examples (1)-(17). Eaton 2019: publisher abstract.
catalog_quote: [Eaton 2018: 12] Stress in Vwanji is predictable and normally falls on the antepenultimate mora of the word. There is no need to mark stress in the orthography. [p. 5] With the exception of ideophones, such as <tuu> ‘thump’ and <swee> ‘shiny, bright’, long vowels in Vwanji occur only in the penultimate syllable of the phonological word. Thus word-initial long vowels are only possible in disyllabic words. [Eaton 2020: 66] Vwanji also stands out in another typological way in contrast to its immediate neighbours as it is not a tone language, but rather has a system of predictable stress placement based on mora count. [fn. 5, p. 67] In the transcription of the sentence examples, stress is marked in words of more than one syllable. Vowel length (which typically only occurs in the penultimate syllable) is indicated by IPA length mark (ː). [examples, Eaton 2020] ʊ-mʊ-ˈɣoːsi, mʊ-ˈloːma, a-ka-ˈtoːl-a, a-lʲaˈ-tol-ile, paˈlʷakɪlo, kʊ-paˈpamʊk-a, a-ˈkinul-a, na-ˈm̩-pok-a, ˈkʊ-la, ˈkuːti. [Eaton 2019 abstract] Vwanji (Bantu G66, Tanzania) has a seven-vowel system with contrastive length and predictable stress on the antepenultimate mora of the word.

new_statements.citation: Eaton, Helen. 2018 [2013]. Vwanji orthography statement. SIL International, Tanzania. 32 pp.
new_statements.locator: Section 3 'Stress', p. 12 (corroborated by Eaton 2020: 66 and fn.5, file; and by the author's abstract of Eaton 2019 'Vwanji G66', Routledge)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: copies we hold checked under ( present and accurate; no new files downloaded, so it was left unchanged). (1) 32 pp., the PDF's metadata creation 2018-12-11; Appendix 2 revision log 2013-12-12.. 2018-09-17, 'Put together by Helen Eaton'): extracted text of p.12 shows the heading '3. Stress' followed verbatim by 'Stress in Vwanji is predictable and normally falls on the antepenultimate mora of the word. There is no need to mark stress in the orthography.' Surrounding sections read: p.5 sec. 2.2 'With the exception of ideophones.. long vowels in Vwanji occur only in the penultimate syllable of the phonological word'; compensatory lengthening before NC and after Cw/Cy is not phonemic length; pp…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is predictable, not lexical and not tonal: it falls on the syllable containing the third mora from the end of the word. Since phonemic long vowels occur only in the penultimate syllable (orthography statement p.5), this means: penultimate stress when the penult has a long vowel (mʊ-ˈloːma, ʊ-ˈmʷaːna, ˈβʷaːᶮɟi), antepenultimate stress otherwise (paˈlʷakɪlo, a-ˈkinul-a, si-ka-poˈsani-a); disyllables are stressed on the first syllable (ˈkʊ-la, ˈʊɟʊ). Vwanji is explicitly described as not a tone language, unlike its G60 neighbours.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said about secondary stress in any of the three sources.
new_statements.exceptions: The rule is hedged with 'normally'; no specific exceptions are listed. Ideophones (e.g. tuu, swee) may have long vowels outside the penult (p.5). Compensatory lengthening before NC and after Cw/Cy is not counted as phonemic length (p.5). Eaton 2020 fn.9 notes one irregular shortened verb form /ˈnapela/ but not as a stress exception.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word: the orthography statement (pp.23-24) uses the single stress pattern as a diagnostic that reduplicated forms and -nya + noun sequences constitute one phonological word; a noun + possessive determiner forms a phonological phrase in which penult long vowels shorten (p.6). Examples in Eaton 2020 are running narrative text with stress marked per word, so the rule is not limited to citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: All three sources are by Helen Eaton (SIL) and describe Vwanji as spoken in Makete District (Kipengere Mountains), Njombe Region = Glottolog vwan1235 exactly. The orthography statement notes dialect-dependent vowel-harmony variation but states the stress rule for the language as a whole. Neighbouring G60 relatives (Kinga, Bena, Sangu) are explicitly contrasted as restricted-tone languages, so the statement must not be generalised to them.
